_about: RPE Unit 4 (Open access publishing) with the focus on journal finders, as asked by the course teacher. Live phone questions come from ace-live (bank.json); this source holds them as check slides so the speaker script and the deck share slide numbers. Facts checked on 21 Oct 2026 against the sources in the reference list.
title: Where should my paper go? Journal finders, hands on
desc: A about 30-minute interactive coursework session on open access publishing and journal finder tools (JANE, Elsevier JournalFinder, Springer Nature Journal Suggester), with live phone questions, a live demo and an offline simulated finder.
design: Field guide: warm paper, deep ink, one open-access amber accent, compass-like match bars. The loud idea is the publisher switch in the simulated finder.
script_design: Same field-guide look as the slides, plain and scannable while presenting.
audience: PhD scholars from mixed disciplines and the course teacher
goal: every scholar leaves able to run a journal finder and verify its suggestions

slides.notes: Good morning, everyone. My topic is open access, and one very practical question. Where should my paper go? [pause] Today we will try real journal finders, play with a fake one, and answer six quick questions on your phones. Yes, phones are allowed today.
slides.next: First, get your phones out and join.
script: Good morning, everyone. [pause]

Raise your hand if you have ever finished a paper and then thought, now where do I send this? [pause] Keep your hand up if you asked your supervisor first. [pause] Good. That is normal. Today we add a method on top of that.
Here is the plan. Two minutes on open access. Then how journal finders work. A live demo. A fake finder you can play with. And then how to check that a journal is real. [pause]
And yes, today you are allowed to use your phone in class. Enjoy it. It may not happen again.

Wait for most answers, then reveal. Read the top two answers aloud. Say: both are fine starting points. By the end of today, you will have a better method to add to them.

slides.label: Four routes
slides.headline: Open access means anyone can read your paper, by one of four routes

visual.html:
GoldJournal opens itFree to read, may charge an APC
GreenYou archive itA version in a repository, often after an embargo
DiamondFree both waysNo fee to read, no fee to publish
HybridPay to openA subscription journal opens one article for a fee

slides.over_reason: Four routes are the whole of 4.1. Each card is one short line.
slides.src: Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002). Action Plan for Diamond Open Access (2022).
slides.notes: Open access simply means anyone can read your paper online, free. There are four routes. [pause] Gold, the journal opens it. Green, you put a copy in a repository. Diamond, free for readers and authors. Hybrid, you pay to open one article.
slides.next: Quick check on your phones.
script: Think of a paper like a movie. [pause] Gold is a free movie on YouTube. The journal makes it free, but sometimes the author pays a fee, called the APC, article processing charge.
Green is when the cinema shows it, but you are allowed to keep your own copy at home, usually after some months. That waiting time is called an embargo. [pause]
Diamond is the best deal. Free to watch and free to make. Usually run by universities or societies.
Hybrid is a subscription journal where you can pay extra to make your one paper free. [pause] So the route you choose also changes your budget.

slides.label: Q: which route
slides.headline: Your subscription journal lets you post the accepted manuscript in a repository after 12 months. Which route is that?
slides.notes: Quick check. Your journal is subscription, but it lets you post your accepted manuscript in a repository after 12 months. Which route is that? [pause] Answer: green.
slides.next: Now, how do you find the right journal in the first place?
script: Let them answer. Then reveal. [pause]
Say: Green. The journal stays closed, but you keep a legal free copy after the embargo. Good news for scholars without a big budget.

slides.notes: A journal finder is like matchmaking for your paper. [pause] You paste your abstract. The tool picks out the important words. It compares them with papers each journal has already published. The closest journals come to the top.
slides.next: Quick check on your phones.
slides.over_reason: The mechanism is four short steps, shown as a sequence.
script: You know how a shopping app says, people who bought this also bought that? [pause] A journal finder does something similar for papers.

Step one, you paste your title and abstract. Step two, the tool turns it into important keywords, with weights. Step three, it compares those words with thousands of published papers. Step four, journals that published papers like yours come to the top. [pause]
So the tool matches words. It does not read your paper like a reviewer. Keep that in mind. It will matter in ten minutes.

slides.label: Q: whose shelf
slides.headline: You paste your abstract into Elsevier JournalFinder. Which journals can it suggest?
slides.notes: Phones again. You paste your abstract into Elsevier JournalFinder. Which journals can it suggest? [pause] The answer is B. Elsevier journals only.
slides.next: So read the label on each finder.
script: Let them answer, then reveal. [pause]
Say: Elsevier's finder only shows Elsevier journals. Springer's finder only shows Springer journals. It is like asking a Maruti showroom which car is best. [pause] You know the answer before you ask.

slides.headline: JANE shows a tag beside a suggested journal. Which tag should raise your trust?
slides.notes: JANE shows tags next to journals. Which tag should raise your trust? [pause] Answer A. Indexed in MEDLINE. Fast publication and email invitations are marketing, not quality.

Say: MEDLINE is a curated list. Someone checked those journals. Fast publication is not a quality sign. It is a sales line.

script: Ask first: which one would you check first? [pause] Most people say indexing.
Tap 1, scope. Say: the best first check is scope. If your paper does not fit, it comes back in a week. That is called a desk rejection, and it is not as relaxing as it sounds. [pause]

Tap 2 to 6, one line each. Board: search two names on Google. Indexing: check the database yourself. Fees: should be clear before you submit. Review in 72 hours: red flag. Recent issues: would you cite these papers?

questions.q: Which finder should a social science or humanities scholar use?
questions.a: JANE covers PubMed, so it suits biomedical work. Use the publisher finders (Elsevier, Springer Nature) for other fields, and cross-check in Scopus or Web of Science and DOAJ.

questions.q: Is a journal with an APC predatory?
questions.a: No. Many genuine gold open access journals charge an APC. Predatory journals charge without real peer review. Check DOAJ and the database indexing, not the fee alone.
Jisc combined Sherpa Romeo, Juliet and Fact into Open Policy Finder in 2024. It shows what version you may self-archive and when.

questions.q: Since the UGC-CARE list is gone, how do we judge a journal?
questions.a: UGC asked institutions to set up their own evaluation using its suggested parameters, such as editorial board, peer review policy, ethics and visibility. Check your university's current rule.

questions.q: Do journal finders keep my abstract private?
questions.a: Each tool has its own terms. Do not paste unpublished results you are not ready to share. Read the tool's privacy note first.

questions.q: Should I just choose the highest Impact Factor?
questions.a: No. Scope fit decides acceptance. A good fit in a solid indexed journal beats a desk rejection from a famous one.
SPPU's Centre for Publication Ethics ran the screening protocol behind the UGC-CARE list. Its current status should be checked, since the CARE list was discontinued in 2025.
